coin-flip.a1: Yes. Each flip takes one random bit from your browser's cryptographic random number generator (Web Crypto), so heads and tails each have exactly a 50% chance and earlier flips never affect the next one.
coin-flip.q2: Can I flip several coins at once?
coin-flip.a2: Yes. Pick 10, 100 or 1,000 coins under Coins per flip. The result says how many came up heads and tails, and every coin is added to the counts.
coin-flip.q3: Why do I sometimes get many heads in a row?
coin-flip.a3: Streaks are normal. In 100 fair flips the longest run of one side is usually 5 to 7. The Longest streak line shows yours.
coin-flip.a4: Yes. Press Space or Enter to flip when the page is scrolled to the coin and no field or link is focused.
coin-flip.a5: Counts and history stay until you press Reset or close the tab. Nothing is uploaded or stored.

guitar-tuner.q1: How do I tune my guitar with this tuner?
guitar-tuner.a1: Press Start tuner and allow the microphone. Pluck one string and let it ring. The tuner shows the nearest string and a needle: left means flat (tighten the string), right means sharp (loosen it). Stop when the needle is in the green zone.
guitar-tuner.q2: What are the notes of standard guitar tuning?
guitar-tuner.a2: From the thickest string to the thinnest: E2, A2, D3, G3, B3 and E4 (82.41, 110, 146.83, 196, 246.94 and 329.63 Hz at A4 = 440 Hz).
guitar-tuner.q3: Can I tune a bass, ukulele or violin?
guitar-tuner.a3: Yes. Pick it under Instrument: 4- and 5-string bass, ukulele (G C E A), violin, cello, alternate guitar tunings such as drop D, half step down, DADGAD and open G, or Chromatic for any note.
guitar-tuner.a4: It is the pitch every other note is worked out from. Almost all music uses 440 Hz. Change it to tune to a piano or recording that sits a little higher or lower, such as 442 Hz or 432 Hz.
guitar-tuner.a5: No. The microphone is analysed in this tab only and nothing is recorded or sent. Close the tab or press Stop to turn the microphone off.

factors.q1: How do I find all the factors of a number?
factors.a1: Type the number. The page lists every divisor from smallest to largest, the factor pairs that multiply to the number and how many divisors there are.
factors.a2: Writing a number as a product of prime numbers, for example 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Every whole number above 1 has exactly one prime factorization.
factors.q3: How do I know if a number is prime?
factors.a3: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. The page says whether your number is prime and shows the primes just below and above it. 1 is neither prime nor composite.
factors.q4: How large a number can it factor?
factors.a4: Any whole number up to 18 digits, exactly. It uses a deterministic Miller–Rabin prime test and Pollard's rho method, so even large numbers take a fraction of a second.
factors.q5: How is the number of divisors worked out?
factors.a5: Add 1 to each exponent in the prime factorization and multiply: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ has (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 24 divisors.

lcm-gcf.q1: How do I find the LCM and GCF?
lcm-gcf.a1: Type two or more whole numbers separated by commas or spaces. The least common multiple (LCM) and greatest common factor (GCF) appear at once, with the working.
lcm-gcf.q2: Is GCF the same as GCD or HCF?
lcm-gcf.a2: Yes. Greatest common factor (GCF), greatest common divisor (GCD) and highest common factor (HCF) are three names for the largest number that divides all of them.
lcm-gcf.q3: How do prime factors give the LCM and GCF?
lcm-gcf.a3: Factor each number into primes. The GCF takes each prime that is in every number, at its lowest power; the LCM takes every prime at its highest power. For 12, 18 and 30: GCF = 2 × 3 = 6, LCM = 2² × 3² × 5 = 180.
lcm-gcf.a4: For two numbers, divide the larger by the smaller and keep the remainder; repeat with the smaller number and the remainder until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the GCF. The page shows each step.
lcm-gcf.q5: When do I need the LCM?
lcm-gcf.a5: To add fractions (the LCM of the denominators is the lowest common denominator) and to find when repeating events line up, such as buses every 12 and 18 minutes meeting every 36 minutes.

coin-flip.lead: Flip a fair coin, or a thousand, in one tap. Nothing is uploaded.

guitar-tuner.lead: Tune a guitar, bass, ukulele or violin with your microphone. Nothing is uploaded.
guitar-tuner.s1b: Pick your instrument and tuning, then press Start tuner and allow the microphone.
guitar-tuner.s2b: Let it ring. The tuner shows the nearest string, its frequency and how many cents it is off.
guitar-tuner.s3t: Turn the peg until it is green
guitar-tuner.s3b: Needle left: flat, tighten. Needle right: sharp, loosen. In tune is within ±5 cents. Play reference sounds the string's note.

factors.lead: Find every factor of a number and whether it is prime. Nothing is uploaded.
factors.s1b: Type a whole number up to 18 digits, or tap an example.
factors.s2b: See if the number is prime, its prime factorization such as 2³ × 3² × 5, and the primes just below and above it.
factors.s3b: Every divisor is listed in order, with the factor pairs, the number of divisors and their sum.

lcm-gcf.lead: Find the least common multiple and greatest common factor of several numbers. Nothing is uploaded.
lcm-gcf.s1b: Type 2 to 20 whole numbers separated by commas or spaces.
lcm-gcf.s2b: Both appear at once, and the page says when the numbers are coprime (GCF 1).
lcm-gcf.s3b: Each number's prime factors show how the GCF and LCM are built. For two numbers, Euclid's algorithm is shown step by step.
